questions.question: What is the basic customer acquisition cost formula?
questions.answer_summary: Total marketing (and sales) spend divided by the number of new customers acquired in that period; e.g. $500 ÷ 10 customers = $50 CAC.

questions.question: What costs should be included when calculating CAC?
questions.answer_summary: Marketing software subscriptions, staff compensation, advertising fees, promotional discounts, content creation, and sales support costs — omitting salaries is called out as a common distortion.

questions.question: Does CAC only count brand-new customers?
questions.answer_summary: Yes — the metric is meant to track only new customers, and conflating repeat/retained customers into the count skews the number.

questions.question: What is considered a good LTV to CAC ratio?
questions.answer_summary: A ratio between 3:1 and 5:1 is generally considered healthy; below that suggests unsustainable acquisition spend, and well above it can suggest under-investment in growth.

questions.question: What is the CAC formula per MetricHQ?
questions.answer_summary: Sum of sales costs plus marketing costs, divided by the count of new customers.

questions.question: Does CAC vary by customer segment?
questions.answer_summary: Yes — enterprise customers typically require a substantially different (usually higher) acquisition investment than smaller customers, so aggregate CAC can mask real differences.

questions.question: Is it normal for CAC to rise during a growth phase?
questions.answer_summary: Yes, CAC may intentionally increase during deliberate growth pushes, but many businesses fail to account for this strategic context when judging the number.
